text.en:
Maya arranged marbles in tidy rows: 1, then 3 in a triangle, then 6 in a bigger triangle.
"Wait—are number patterns actually pictures in disguise?" she asked.

Mathematics is the search for patterns—both in numbers and in shapes! Counting numbers (1, 2, 3, 4...), odd numbers (1, 3, 5, 7...) and even numbers (2, 4, 6, 8...) are number sequences.
When we arrange dots as shapes, patterns come alive: squares use 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 dots (n × n), and triangles use 1, 3, 6, 10, 15 dots.
Looking at dot pictures explains amazing links! Adding consecutive odd numbers starting from 1 always builds a square L-layer by L-layer: 1 + 3 = 4, 1 + 3 + 5 = 9, 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16!
Maths becomes exciting when you spot how sequences of numbers and pictures match step for step.
Everyday sequences include counting numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, odd numbers 1, 3, 5, 7, and even numbers 2, 4, 6, 8.
Now arrange dots in tiny squares: 1 dot, 2×2 = 4 dots, 3×3 = 9 dots, 4×4 = 16 dots, 5×5 = 25 dots—the square numbers!
Look at L-shaped borders around each square: start with 1, add 3 to get 4, add 5 to get 9, add 7 to get 16!

board.text: Sum of first n odd numbers = n²

text.en: That picture proves why 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 = 25 without even adding tediously: there are 5 odd numbers, so the sum is 5×5 = 25!
Next stack dots like a bowling triangle: 1 dot, 1+2 = 3 dots, 1+2+3 = 6 dots, 1+2+3+4 = 10 dots, 15 dots—triangular numbers!
Join two touching triangular dot pictures—say 3 + 6, or 6 + 10—and watch what snaps together: 9 and 16, always a square number!
Watch powers too: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 (powers of 2 double each time), and cube numbers 1, 8, 27, 64 build 3D blocks!
And Koch snowflakes or stacked triangles multiply perimeters in shape sequences where patterns stay predictable far ahead.

board.text: Shape patterns grow cleanly by rules

text.en: Whenever a sequence puzzles you, draw dot rows or square borders—seeing the picture makes the rule unforgettable!

board.text: Draw dots to understand number rules

problem.en: Find the sum 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11 using the square dot pattern instead of long addition.

text.en: Count how many consecutive odd numbers start from 1.
Remember each new odd number adds an L-shaped layer to grow the next square.

why.en: 6 layers form a 6 × 6 square of dots.

prompt.en: How can two triangular dot numbers build a square number?

requiredIdeas.en: Add two side-by-side triangular numbers like 6 and 10.
Their dots fit neatly to form a 4×4 = 16 square.

commonMisconceptions.en: Adding any two random numbers always gives a square.

points.en: Sum of first n odd numbers = n².
Two consecutive triangular numbers add up to a square number.
